summary: Defines three mechanisms for getting a URI that points to a user's calendar and free or busy times, for use with vCard and LDAP. It is a standards-track document at the proposed standard level.

eli5.summary: It is a way to put a link to your calendar in your contact card so others can check when you are free.

questions: how to find a persons calendar in ldap
how to find free busy time with ldap
subtitle: How to publish links to your calendar and busy times in a contact card or a directory entry.

tldr.problem: To invite someone to an event, a calendar program needs that person's calendar address and ideally a way to see when they are busy, but there was no standard place to find those links.
tldr.mechanism: The memo defines four kinds of calendar URI and three ways to share them: hand them over manually, put them in a vCard through four new properties, or look them up in an LDAP directory through a new object class and eight new attributes.
tldr.outcome: A calendar user agent can find a person's calendar, free/busy data and event-request address from a contact card or a directory. The RFC has since been updated by RFC 6350.

today: RFC 2739 is a Proposed Standard that has been updated by RFC 6350. The text here does not say how widely these properties and attributes are used.

sections.title: Four Kinds of Calendar URI
sections.content:
Before an organizer can schedule an event, the calendar program (a calendar user agent, or CUA) needs each attendee's calendar address. Seeing an attendee's busy time first tells the organizer whether that person is likely to be free. RFC 2739 gives the CUA a way to find a URI for a user's calendar and free/busy time.

The memo defines four classes of URI. FBURL is the free/busy URI: a transport-independent place to get a user's busy time. Fetching it by FTP or HTTP returns an iCalendar object holding one or more VFREEBUSY components. It is recommended that the previous six weeks of busy time be published there, and that a file be named with the extension ifb to tell it apart from an ordinary ics calendar file.

CALURI is a place to retrieve a published snapshot of a user's entire calendar. An HTTP URI should return a text/calendar body, and an FTP URI should point to a file with an ics extension. CAPURI is a protocol independent location for talking to the user's whole calendar; how to use it was left to a future Calendar Access Protocol specification of the IETF CALSCH Working Group. CALADRURI is the location to which event requests for the user should be sent.
sections.eli5: Think of four labels on a door: one says where to see when I am busy, one says where to read my whole calendar, one says how to chat with my calendar, and one says where to drop invitations.

sections.title: Default and Multiple Calendars
sections.content:
A user may have more than one calendar, and so more than one URI. To keep things simple for clients, the memo introduces a default calendar: the one the user has designated for other people to look at when they access the calendar or retrieve free/busy time.

The default calendar may contain rolled-up information from all of the user's other calendars. The other calendars may exist only for organizational purposes.
sections.eli5: If you keep a school calendar and a soccer calendar, you pick one as the main one that friends should check first.

sections.title: Getting the URIs to Other People
sections.content:
The memo describes three ways to pass these URIs along. The simplest is manual transfer: tell someone out of band, for example verbally, in an e-mail message, or printed on a paper business card, and they type the URIs into their calendar software.

The second is a vCard. Many e-mail clients can attach a vCard to every outgoing message, which spreads the URIs transparently. A receiving client with an integrated vCard database can look up calendar URIs for people whose vCards it stores.

The third is a directory lookup with LDAP. The memo says URIs found this way should generally be considered more up to date than URIs in locally stored vCards.
sections.eli5: You can tell a friend your calendar address, hand over a contact card, or let them look you up in a big phone book. The phone book is usually the freshest.

sections.title: vCard Extensions
sections.content:
The vCard specification has no way to hold calendar URIs, so the memo adds four properties: CALURI, CAPURI, CALADRURI and FBURL. A vCard may carry one or more of each, and one may be marked as the default by adding the PREF parameter.

Each property holds a single URI value and uses 8bit encoding. The memo gives registration text for each. CALURI should point to an iCalendar snapshot of the user's calendar store, and FBURL to a snapshot of the last six weeks of busy time.
sections.eli5: A contact card gets four new boxes to write calendar addresses in, and a star can mark which address is the favorite.

sections.title: LDAP Schema Extensions
sections.content:
For directories, the memo defines one auxiliary object class, calEntry, and eight attributes. Four hold the default values: calCalURI (snapshot of the default calendar), calFBURL (default busy time), calCAPURI (a URI to communicate with the user's calendar) and calCalAdrURI (where event requests go).

Four more are multi-valued and hold the user's other URIs: calOtherCalURIs, calOtherFBURLs, calOtherCAPURIs and calOtherCalAdrURIs. There is no predetermined order to the values in a multi-valued attribute.

Every attribute uses the IA5String syntax with caseIgnoreMatch for equality and substring matching, and has USAGE userApplications.
sections.eli5: In the big phone book, each person gets slots for their main calendar addresses, plus extra slots that can hold several more, in any order.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The memo says standard vCard and LDAP security rules apply and that the extensions add no special security issues. It still lists three cautions.

  • LDAP servers may let anonymous clients refresh entries they did not create. Servers may require a client to bind first, which affects performance and scalability.
  • A vCard may have been created by someone other than the person it describes, so recipients should be sure of its source.
  • Information that clients supplied to a directory may be out of date. An IP address, for example, may have been reassigned to a different host.
sections.eli5: A contact card could have been written by someone else, and an address in the phone book might be old, so check before you trust it.
